messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai had always been proud of his culinary skills, whipping up intricate dishes with ease in the high-pressure kitchen of his restaurant. But that was before the night he was raped by a colleague after a late-night shift. The event shattered Kai's sense of self, leaving him feeling dirty and contaminated. He couldn't shake the thought that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him – cooking with passion, leading his team with confidence. As Kai struggled to make sense of what had happened, he found himself pushing away memories of the assault before they could fully surface. He'd start to recall a detail, only to suddenly feel overwhelmed and distracted. The fragments he did manage to grasp were jumbled and out of sequence, like a recipe with missing ingredients and garbled instructions. Kai couldn't help but wonder if this disjointedness was a manifestation of his own guilt – as if his mind was deliberately obscuring the truth from him. The feeling of contamination seeped into every aspect of Kai's life. He started to avoid social gatherings, fearing that others could sense his 'dirtiness'. Even in the kitchen, where he once felt most at home, the smells and sounds now triggered anxiety and self-doubt. "What if they can smell it on me?" he'd think, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. Kai became withdrawn, barely able to muster the energy to create new dishes or manage his team. As time passed, Kai's negative appraisals began to shape his memories of the event. He started to recall moments that reinforced his sense of powerlessness and worthlessness. The more he dwelled on these memories, the more distorted they became – a self-reinforcing cycle that further entrenched his feelings of contamination and inadequacy. His life felt destroyed, like a recipe book with torn-out pages and illegible notes. The strain began to show in Kai's relationships and work performance. His ex-wife, whom he'd divorced a few years prior, noticed the change in him and tried to reach out, but Kai pushed her away. His staff at the restaurant grew concerned about his erratic behavior, but Kai just shrugged it off, unsure of how to articulate the turmoil brewing inside. It wasn't until Kai received a notice that his assailant would be working at a nearby restaurant that he realized he needed help. The thought of being in the same culinary community as his attacker sent Kai into a tailspin of anxiety and self-doubt. He knew he couldn't keep living like this, stuck in a cycle of avoidance and negative appraisals. With a deep breath, Kai picked up the phone and made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find a way to reclaim his life – and his passion for cooking – from the darkness that had consumed him.
